judge_reasoning: Watkins & Dayan (1992) "Q-learning" is a well-known, canonical reinforcement learning paper published in Machine Learning, vol. 8, issue 3-4, pages 279-292. Search results (Springer, Gatsby/UCL author page, ResearchGate) confirm exact match on title, authors, year, and venue with the cited pagination.

Three targeted web searches (title+authors+year, exact title phrase "Effectiveness of MCEDF", and venue+authors+year) found no evidence anywhere of a work titled "Interest Groups and the Kyoto Protocol: The Effectiveness of MCEDF" by Winkler & Beaumont. The cited venue (Centre for International Environmental Studies, Graduate Institute Geneva) is real and was founded around 2010, but no publication by these authors with this title exists in its output or anywhere else on the open web; "MCEDF" also does not correspond to any known Kyoto Protocol mechanism or entity. No work matches the cited title anywhere on the open web, satisfying §6 FABRICATED criterion (a).
Utility Air Regulatory Group v. EPA is a real U.S. Supreme Court case, 573 U.S. 302 (2014), decided June 23, 2014, matching the cited case name and year exactly.

No paper titled "GAFF, an amorphous force field for the simulation of organic molecular solids" by Klein, Jorgensen & Feng exists. The real GAFF paper is "Development and testing of a general amber force field" by Wang, Wolf, Caldwell, Kollman & Case (2004), published in the Journal of Computational Chemistry 25(9), 1157-1174 (DOI 10.1002/jcc.20035) — a completely different title, author byline, and venue (not Journal of Chemical Physics). This is not a metadata error on the real work; the cited title and authors do not identify the real GAFF paper at all.

Watkins, C.J.C.H. and Dayan, P., "Q-learning," Machine Learning, vol. 8, pp. 279-292, 1992, is confirmed via Springer, ResearchGate, and the Gatsby (Dayan's own) publication page. Title, authors, year, and venue all match exactly.

Adams Express Co. v. Croninger, 226 U.S. 491 (1913) is a well-documented U.S. Supreme Court case (decided January 6, 1913) confirmed by GovInfo, CourtListener, Justia, and FindLaw, addressing carrier liability under the Carmack Amendment. Case name, reporter citation, and year all match exactly.

Exact match confirmed: "The Elements of Statistical Learning: Data Mining, Inference, and Prediction, Second Edition" by Trevor Hastie, Robert Tibshirani, and Jerome Friedman is a well-known Springer Series in Statistics textbook (ISBN 9780387848570), verified via Springer, Amazon, and other listings.
Planned Parenthood of Southeastern Pennsylvania v. Casey, 505 U.S. 833, was decided by the U.S. Supreme Court on June 29, 1992, matching the cited case name and year exactly.

29 U.S.C. § 2615 is a real, correctly identified provision of the Family and Medical Leave Act (Title 29, Chapter 28, "Prohibited acts"), confirmed via Justia and the official U.S. Code (house.gov) sources. The citation's title, statutory section, and venue (United States Code) all match.

Martin v. Boise was decided by the Ninth Circuit (920 F.3d 584, 9th Cir. 2019); the Supreme Court denied certiorari on December 16, 2019, and never issued a merits decision, so no "590 U.S. ___ (2020)" opinion exists. The cited reporter/volume/year attributes a nonexistent Supreme Court ruling to a case that in fact never received one, which is positive evidence of non-existence per §6(a).

A paper titled exactly "Particle Swarm Optimization: An Overview" exists, but it is by Poli, Kennedy & Blackwell, published 2007 in Swarm Intelligence (DOI 10.1007/s11721-007-0002-0) — not by "Misra and Pati (2012)" as cited. No evidence of any Misra/Pati 2012 paper with this or a similar title was found across three searches. The byline and year given do not match the real work the title points to, and the mismatch (different authors entirely, 5-year gap) is far beyond a typo/metadata error, so this is an EXISTENT_WRONG_ID-style fabrication rather than REAL-with-metadata-error.

The cited title "Wikipedia:Entertainment accuracy" does not correspond to any real Wikipedia page, guideline, or other identifiable work. Two web searches found no matching page, and directly fetching https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Entertainment_accuracy returned HTTP 404 Not Found, confirming the page does not exist.

The citation exactly matches a real, well-known paper: Jonathan Frankle and Michael Carbin, "The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis: Finding Sparse, Trainable Neural Networks," presented at ICLR 2019. Title, authors, and year all match precisely, confirmed via ICLR's official virtual poster page and MIT's open-access repository.

The exact title "The Health Benefits of Urban Nature: How Much Do We Need?" is a real paper by Shanahan, Fuller, Bush, Lin & Gaston, published in BioScience 65(5):476-485 (2015) -- not by Frumkin et al. and not in Environment and Behavior (2017). The cited byline (Frumkin, Bratman, Breslow, Cochran, Kahn, Sallis, Simpson) and venue instead match a different real Frumkin-led paper, "Nature Contact and Human Health: A Research Agenda" (Environmental Health Perspectives, 2017), which has a completely different title and partly different author list. The wrong byline/venue names a different real paper, matching the EXISTENT_WRONG_ID FABRICATED criterion.

Bayer Healthcare LLC v. Baxalta Inc., 989 F.3d 964 (Fed. Cir. 2021) is a real, verifiable Federal Circuit decision (No. 19-2418, decided March 1, 2021, on appeal from D. Del.), confirmed by Justia, Google Scholar, and multiple law-firm case summaries. The case caption, reporter citation, and year all match exactly.

The citation provides only a generic topic phrase ("Progestin-only contraceptive implants") with no author, year, venue, or DOI to anchor it to a specific work. Searches surface many real articles/reviews/topic pages on this general subject (PubMed, UpToDate, WHO, FSRH guidelines, ScienceDirect) but none with this exact title and no way to determine which specific work, if any, is being cited given the total absence of identifying metadata. No positive evidence of non-existence, and no exact match to confirm a specific real work either.

Two independent web searches confirm McGehee v. Berryhill exists as a 2019 District of Massachusetts case (docket 1:18-cv-11389), reported at 386 F. Supp. 3d 80, an SSA disability benefits case addressing RFC/emotional support animal issues. Case name, reporter citation, and year all match the cited attribution exactly.

No case titled "Nakashima v. Department of Defense" appears in Federal Circuit records or general web search. Additionally, the cited reporter "F.4th" (Federal Reporter, Fourth Series) did not begin publication until June 2021, making a citation of "829 F.4th 4352 (Fed. Cir. 2019)" anachronistic and impossible as written -- positive evidence the citation does not exist rather than a garbled real case.

The Sherman Act (Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890, 15 U.S.C. §§ 1-7) is a well-established, real US federal statute; no other identifying metadata was provided that could point to a different work, so the citation unambiguously identifies this real law.

Schoof's algorithm is a well-established, real algorithm for counting points on elliptic curves over finite fields, published by René Schoof in 1985. The citation's author surname "Schoof" and title "Schoof's algorithm" unambiguously identify this real, widely-documented work (confirmed via Wikipedia and multiple academic sources).

WebSearch confirms Amyndas Pharmaceuticals, S.A. v. Zealand Pharma A/S, 48 F.4th 18 (1st Cir. 2022), decided September 2, 2022, Case No. 21-1781, is a real First Circuit case (trade secrets/CDA dispute), matching the cited case name, reporter citation, venue, and year exactly. Confirmed via Justia, Leagle, and vLex.

No case titled "Nakashima v. City of Sacramento" exists in Ninth Circuit records from 2021 or any other year; two targeted web searches returned no matching case, only unrelated Nakashima-surname results. Additionally the citation itself is internally impossible: F.4th (Federal Reporter, Fourth Series) only began publication in 2021 at volume 1, so a 2021 case could not appear at volume 866. This is positive evidence the citation does not exist (§6 FABRICATED criterion a).

Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta is a real U.S. Supreme Court case, decided 597 U.S. 629 (2022) on June 29, 2022, addressing state jurisdiction to prosecute non-Indians for crimes against Indians in Indian country. Case name and year exactly match the citation.

A real paper with this exact title exists (Backenköhler, Bortolussi, Wolf, "Control Variates for Stochastic Simulation of Chemical Reaction Networks," CMSB 2019, arXiv:1905.00854), but the cited authors (Greenberg, Mucha) and year (2015) do not match it at all -- this is not a garbled version of the real byline but an entirely different set of names, and no Greenberg/Mucha paper on this topic exists anywhere in search results. This is the EXISTENT_WRONG_ID failure mode under §6(b): the title picks out a real work, but the attribution names a different authorship.

The title "A Biterm Topic Model for Short Texts" is real, but it belongs to Xiaohui Yan, Jiafeng Guo, Yanyan Lan, and Xueqi Cheng, published at WWW 2013 (ACM DOI 10.1145/2488388.2488514) — not to Yankai Lin, Shujian Huang, and Zhiyuan Liu at KDD 2012 as cited. The given authors are a completely different, non-overlapping set of real researchers with no traceable 2012 paper matching this title, and the venue is also wrong, so this is a wrong byline/venue attached to someone else's real paper rather than a minor metadata error.

Lucky Brand Dungarees, Inc. v. Marcel Fashions Group, Inc. is a real U.S. Supreme Court case (docket 18-1086), argued January 13, 2020 and decided May 14, 2020, unanimous opinion by Justice Sotomayor on defense preclusion. The citation 590 U.S. 405 (2020) matches the case as confirmed by Justia and SupremeCourt.gov, which list it as 590 U.S. ___ (2020).

The cited work matches a real, well-known study: Billioti de Gage S et al., "Benzodiazepine use and risk of Alzheimer's disease: case-control study," BMJ 2012;345:e6231 (published 27 Sept 2012), which found benzodiazepine use associated with increased Alzheimer's disease risk. Title, first-author surname, year, and venue all match exactly.

Three WebSearch queries (title+authors+year, journal-domain-restricted, and volume/collection-restricted) found many real Kaufmann/Schaible tuberculosis-immunology papers and the CSHPM Tuberculosis subject collection Kaufmann co-edits, but no result matching this exact title "Immune Response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis" by Kaufmann and Schaible in Cold Spring Harbor Perspectives in Medicine 2011. No definitive evidence of the work's existence or non-existence was found within the search budget.
The McCarran-Ferguson Act is codified at 15 U.S.C. §§ 1011-1015, confirmed via Cornell LII and govinfo.gov, exactly matching the cited title and statutory citation.

New York v. Quarles is a real, well-documented U.S. Supreme Court case, 467 U.S. 649, decided June 12, 1984, establishing the "public safety" exception to Miranda. The case name and year exactly match the citation under review.

Three targeted WebSearch queries (exact title; title+authors+year+venue; authors+topic) found no trace of a 1996 British Journal of General Practice article titled "Burnout in general practice: a study of its prevalence and relationship to job characteristics" by Rogers, Freedy, and Castro. Search results returned only unrelated BJGP burnout literature (e.g., Kirwan & Armstrong 1995, Sutherland & Cooper) and unrelated work by Freedy (PTSD/stress research), with no matching title or byline anywhere on the open web, indicating this citation does not exist.

Cheney v. United States District Court for the District of Columbia, 542 U.S. 367 (2004) is a real, well-known Supreme Court case (Vice President Cheney's energy task force mandamus dispute, decided June 24, 2004, opinion by Kennedy). The reporter citation, year, and core case name ("Cheney v. United States District Court") exactly match this real case; only the specified district ("Northern District of California" instead of the correct "District of Columbia") is wrong. This is a venue/metadata error that does not point to any other real case at that citation, so it does not change which work is being cited.

Web search confirms Planet Sub Holdings, Inc. v. State Auto Property & Casualty is a real 8th Circuit case, No. 21-2199, decided June 6, 2022, matching the cited reporter citation 36 F.4th 772 and case name exactly.

The VICTORIA trial (Vericiguat in Patients with Heart Failure and Reduced Ejection Fraction) is a real, well-known Phase 3 trial published in NEJM (Armstrong et al., DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1915928). The actual publication year is 2020, not 2019 as cited, but this is within the taxonomy's ±1 year tolerance for a metadata error that does not change which work is being cited; title and venue unambiguously identify the real work.

CheckMate 143 is a real glioblastoma immunotherapy trial (NCT02017717), but its phase 3 results were published in JAMA Oncology in 2020 (Reardon et al., PMID 32437507), and its phase 1 cohort results were published in Neuro-Oncology Advances in 2022 — no publication of this trial appeared in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2019 or any other year. The cited venue+year combination does not match any real work, so the attribution points to a publication that does not exist.

Lorenzo v. SEC is a real U.S. Supreme Court case (Rule 10b-5 scheme-liability decision, docket 17-1077), decided March 27, 2019 and officially reported at 587 U.S. ___ (2019), not "581 U.S. ___ (2020)" as cited. The case name unambiguously identifies the one real Supreme Court case of that name, so the wrong reporter volume and year (off by one) are metadata errors, not evidence of a different or nonexistent case, per the §6 REAL criteria.

The real PORTEC-2 trial ("Vaginal brachytherapy versus pelvic external beam radiotherapy for patients with endometrial cancer of high-intermediate risk (PORTEC-2)") was published in The Lancet in 2010 (vol 375, pp 816-823), not in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2019. This is not a minor transcription error: the venue is a different journal entirely and the year is off by 9, so the cited attribution does not identify any real NEJM 2019 publication of this trial.

Three WebSearch queries (case name directly, case name + "6th Circuit", and case name + a plausible reporter citation) returned no definitive evidence either confirming or refuting the existence of "Achebe v. KeyBank National Association." No matching case turned up in Justia, FindLaw, or CourtListener results; related KeyBank litigation (Awugah v. Key Bank, Clemmer v. Key Bank, etc.) surfaced instead, but nothing under the Achebe caption. Per the taxonomy, absent positive evidence in either direction within the 3-search budget, the verdict defaults to UNVERIFIABLE.

Three searches for "Exercise therapy for treating rotator cuff disease" (Cochrane, 2017) found no matching review under that title. The real, closely-related Cochrane reviews are "Manual therapy and exercise for rotator cuff disease" (Page MJ et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016, CD012224) and the older "Physiotherapy interventions for shoulder pain" (Green/Buchbinder/Hetrick, 2003) — neither matches the cited title, and neither is dated 2017. The cited title does not correspond to any identifiable real work; this is not a minor transcription typo but a distinct, non-matching title, so no positive identification of a real underlying paper is possible.

Three WebSearch queries (title+author+year, author+journal+year, and PubMed-targeted author search) plus a direct PubMed title-string search for "Patient Expectations and Delays in Seeking Medical Care" returned no matching Eisenberg 1991 Journal of General Internal Medicine article; the closest hit was a differently-titled 1991 PsycNET record ("Expectations and delay in seeking medical care") with unconfirmed authorship, not this title. No positive evidence anywhere on the open web supports this exact title/author/venue/year combination.

Graph Attention Networks by Veličković, Cucurull, Casanova, Romero, Liò, and Bengio is a well-known, widely-cited paper published at ICLR 2018 (also on arXiv:1710.10903). The cited title, authors, year, and venue all match exactly.

HUD v. Facebook refers to a real, well-documented administrative proceeding: HUD charged Facebook in 2019 with violating the Fair Housing Act via discriminatory ad-targeting tools, and the matter concluded with a DOJ/Meta settlement in June 2022. The case name and subject matter are unambiguously identifiable as this real matter; the cited year (2022) plausibly reflects the settlement/resolution date of the same underlying proceeding rather than a different or nonexistent work, which falls within REAL's tolerance for metadata discrepancies that don't change which work is being cited.

No case titled "McDermott International, Inc. v. Wilkins" exists, and the citation "911 F.2d 1133 (5th Cir. 1990)" does not resolve to any such case; three searches found only unrelated 911 F.2d entries and a different real case, Wilander v. McDermott International, Inc., 894 F.2d 406 (5th Cir. 1990) (which led to McDermott Int'l, Inc. v. Wilander, 498 U.S. 337 (1991) at the Supreme Court). The cited party name and reporter citation do not match any real decision, so this is positive evidence of non-existence per §6(a), not a mere metadata error on the real Wilander case.

The citation exactly matches a real paper: Förstermann U, Sessa WC, "Nitric oxide synthases: regulation and function," European Heart Journal, 33(7):829-837, 2012, DOI 10.1093/eurheartj/ehr304, PMID 21890489, confirmed via Oxford Academic and multiple independent citation-index sources.

"In re Lipitor Antitrust Litigation" is a real MDL case decided in D.N.J. in 2018, reported at 336 F.Supp.3d 395 (D.N.J. 2018), confirmed via CourtListener and Leagle. Case name, venue, and year all match exactly.

Davis v. Monroe County Board of Education, 526 U.S. 629 (1999), is a genuine U.S. Supreme Court decision (decided May 24, 1999) confirmed via Justia and Wikipedia; the citation's case name, reporter citation, and year all match exactly.

Three targeted web searches for "Baptiste, Hebrard (2017) Deep Learning for Constraint Satisfaction Problems: A Survey" and for the claimed "IJCAI-17 Workshop on Deep Learning for Artificial Intelligence (DLAI 2017)" returned no matching paper and no evidence the named workshop existed; the actual IJCAI-17 co-located workshop on this topic was "Artificial Intelligence and Constraint Programming," not "DLAI 2017." No work with this title/author/venue combination appears anywhere on the open web, satisfying the FABRICATED(a) no-match criterion.

Three targeted web searches for the exact title "Advanced Oxidation Processes for Water and Wastewater Treatment: A Review" by Feng, Q. (2012, Critical Reviews in Environmental Science and Technology 42(8), 755-804) found no matching work anywhere on the open web. The only closely related hit is a differently titled, differently authored review ("Advanced Oxidation Processes in Water/Wastewater Treatment: Principles and Applications. A Review," Critical Reviews in Environmental Science and Technology, Vol. 44, No. 23, DOI 10.1080/10643389.2013.829765) with different volume/issue/pages and no author named Feng. No paper by a "Feng, Q." with this title, venue, or page range could be located, indicating the cited work does not exist.

Chapra and Canale's actual, well-known textbook is titled "Numerical Methods for Engineers" (no "and Scientists") — confirmed via McGraw-Hill and multiple retailer listings. "Numerical Methods for Engineers and Scientists" is itself a real, existing textbook title, but it belongs to different authors: Amos Gilat & Vish Subramaniam (Wiley), or separately Joe D. Hoffman & Steven Frankel. The cited title exactly names a different real book than the cited authors' actual book, so the title+author pairing does not identify any single existing work (EXISTENT_WRONG_ID pattern).

A Cochrane systematic review titled "Minimally invasive discectomy versus microdiscectomy/open discectomy for symptomatic lumbar disc herniation" by Rasouli MR et al. (2014, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD010328.pub2) matches the cited title/topic exactly on the Cochrane Library site.

County of Sacramento v. Lewis, 523 U.S. 833 (1998), is a real United States Supreme Court case (decided May 26, 1998) addressing substantive due process in high-speed police pursuits. The case name, citation, and year exactly match official sources (Justia, Cornell LII, Library of Congress).

No work matching the title "Aspect-Level Opinion Mining with Dual-Channel Attention Networks" by Amara & Kobayashi exists in the ACL Anthology (which comprehensively indexes ACL 2019 proceedings) or anywhere else on the open web across two targeted searches. No paper by these authors on this topic could be located at all.

The case Brothers and Sisters in Christ, LLC v. Zazzle, Inc. is a real 2022 Eighth Circuit decision (No. 21-1917), confirmed by Justia, CourtListener, and FindLaw, matching the cited title/case name and year exactly.

Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization is a real, well-documented U.S. Supreme Court case, 597 U.S. ___ (2022), decided June 24, 2022, overruling Roe v. Wade. The cited case name is an exact match with no metadata discrepancies.

Three targeted web searches (title, author+year+venue, and author's general JASN 2013 publications) found no work matching "Effects of different hemodialysis modalities on cardiovascular outcomes" by Kasiske et al. in JASN 2013. Search results surfaced related but clearly distinct 2013 JASN nephrology papers (e.g., a vascular-access-type meta-analysis, an "Evidence-Based Cardiology in Hemodialysis Patients" review) but none matching this exact title/author combination, so there is no positive evidence either that the work exists or that it is a misattributed different real work.

CourtListener and Leagle both confirm "In re Lipitor Antitrust Litig.," 336 F. Supp. 3d 395, decided in the District of New Jersey in 2018, matching the cited case name, reporter citation, venue, and year exactly.

Search confirms United States Telecom Ass'n v. FCC, 855 F.3d 381 (D.C. Cir. 2017) is a real case (D.C. Circuit's order denying rehearing en banc in the net neutrality litigation), matching exactly on case name, reporter citation, court, and year per Google Scholar and Leagle.

The Airline Deregulation Act is a real, well-documented US federal statute (Pub. L. 95-504) enacted by the 95th Congress and signed into law by President Carter on October 24, 1978, confirmed via Wikipedia and Congress.gov. The cited title exactly matches this real work with no author, year, or venue attribution to introduce ambiguity.

Employment Division, Department of Human Resources of Oregon v. Smith, 494 U.S. 872 (1990), is a well-documented U.S. Supreme Court case confirmed via Justia, Wikipedia, and the National Constitution Center; the citation's case name, reporter citation, and year exactly match the real decision.

The cited work "Biochemistry" by Jeremy M. Berg, John L. Tymoczko, and Lubert Stryer is a real, well-established textbook first published by W.H. Freeman in 1975 and now in multiple editions, confirmed via Wikipedia, Google Books, and publisher (Macmillan Learning) listings that all show this exact author byline and title.

The Interstate Commerce Act of 1887 is a real, well-documented US federal statute that regulated railroad rates and created the Interstate Commerce Commission, signed into law by President Grover Cleveland on February 4, 1887. Title and year exactly match this well-established historical statute, confirmed by the National Archives, Wikipedia, and other sources.

Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 is a real, well-documented federal statute (42 U.S.C. § 2000d et seq.) prohibiting discrimination based on race, color, and national origin in federally funded programs. DOJ, DOE, DOL, and FTA all confirm its existence and exact title/year, an unambiguous exact match to the citation as given.

Three WebSearch queries (exact title, author+topic terms, exact title alone) returned no record of a paper titled "Wavefront aberrations of the human eye: correlation with vision" by Collins MJ in Journal of Vision 2001. Results surfaced related but distinct Collins publications (e.g., Vision Research 1995/2006 papers on aberrations/myopia) and unrelated papers by other authors, but nothing matching this exact title/author/venue/year combination in either direction. This is insufficient to positively confirm nonexistence (search budget exhausted, no definitive negative evidence), so per §6 this defaults to UNVERIFIABLE rather than FABRICATED.

Three WebSearch queries (exact title, title fragment, and topical search) found no work matching the exact cited title "Cardiac Rhabdomyoma: A Rare Cause of Left Ventricular Outflow Tract Obstruction in a Neonate." The closest real work, an Oxford Academic case report titled "Cardiac rhabdomyoma presenting as left ventricular outflow tract obstruction in a neonate," has different wording and is not a plausible typo-level match. The author field is also degenerate (the token "S." repeated ~200 times), further indicating a non-existent/hallucinated citation rather than a real work with a metadata error.

No case titled "Robinson v. Southeast Florida Health Systems, Inc." appears anywhere in search results (only unrelated Robinson v. ... health-related cases turned up). Additionally the citation is internally impossible: the Federal Reporter, Fourth Series (F.4th) did not begin publication until January 2021, so a "982 F.4th 8335 (11th Cir. 2020)" citation cannot exist for a case decided in 2020, and volume 982 is far beyond any volume reached by F.4th. This is positive evidence of non-existence, not merely absence of confirmation.

Web search for the title "Patent Litigation in the Eastern District of Texas: An Empirical Study" by Fisher & Davis (2018) returns no matching work anywhere; the closest real work on this topic is a different paper by different authors (Love & Yoon, "Predictably Expensive: A Critical Look at Patent Litigation in the Eastern District of Texas"). The cited DOI 10.15779/Z38Q52G does not resolve (404), and that prefix belongs to Berkeley eScholarship journals, not the Texas Law Review, further indicating the citation is invented. No positive evidence for existence anywhere.

A real case titled "United States v. One TRW, Model M14, 7.62 Caliber Rifle" exists, but only at 294 F. Supp. 2d 896 (E.D. Ky. 2003) and on appeal at 441 F.3d 416 (6th Cir. 2006) — no D. Colo. 1977 version exists in any search result. The cited reporter citation "441 F. Supp. 537 (D. Colo. 1977)" actually resolves to an unrelated real case, Gilbert & Bennett Mfg. Co. v. Westinghouse Elec. Corp. (1977), so the citation points at a different real work than its case name implies (EXISTENT_WRONG_ID).

No paper by "Schneider, D. M. & Eccles, J. C. (1957)" titled "The effect of carbon dioxide on spinal reflexes in decapitated cats" exists. The cited DOI (10.1113/jphysiol.1957.sp005696) resolves to a completely different real paper: Granit & Phillips, "Effects on Purkinje cells of surface stimulation of the cerebellum," J Physiol 135(1):73-92 (1957) — the EXISTENT_WRONG_ID failure mode. A similarly titled real paper exists but with different authors/year: Bradley, Schlapp & Spaccarelli, "Effect of carbon dioxide on the spinal reflexes in decapitated cats," J Physiol 111:62P (1956), confirming Schneider/Eccles is not the true byline.

Multiple real federal cases captioned "United States v. Cooper" were decided in 1990 (e.g., 902 F.2d 1570, 6th Cir. 1990, affirming a tax-filing conviction; and 746 F. Supp. 1352, N.D. Ill. 1990). No venue/reporter was given to disambiguate further, but the case name and year exactly match existing real cases, satisfying the REAL criterion.

Three targeted searches for the exact title, and for title+author+year variants, find no paper titled "Effect of intravenous iron sucrose on the hemodynamic response to exercise in patients with chronic heart failure and iron deficiency" by Ponikowski (2016) anywhere on the open web. The closest real Ponikowski-coauthored work on IV iron sucrose in this population is the FERRIC-HF trial (Okonko et al./Ponikowski, JACC 2007/2008), titled "Effect of Intravenous Iron Sucrose on Exercise Tolerance in Anemic and Nonanemic Patients With Symptomatic Chronic Heart Failure and Iron Deficiency" — a different title (exercise tolerance, not hemodynamic response) and a different year (2007/2008, not 2016). The cited title recombines real terms (author, drug, condition) into a title/year that does not correspond to any actual publication, so no real work is uniquely identified by this attribution.

"Collier on Bankruptcy" is a well-documented, singular major legal treatise (LexisNexis, currently edited by Richard Levin and Henry J. Sommer; historically Resnick, Herzog, King, Weintraub, and the original William Collier). No source ties "Jonathan M. Bornstein" to any edition's editorial board, but the title unambiguously identifies this one real treatise regardless of the editor named, so the wrong/unconfirmed editor attribution is a metadata error rather than a pointer to a different real work.

Clarke is a real author active on potato cyst-nematode hatching-factor research in exactly 1966 (Clarke & Widdowson, Biochemical Journal 98:862-868, "The hatching factor of the potato-root eelworm"; also Clarke & Shepherd 1966 in Nature and Annals of Applied Biology on related hatching-agent topics), but three searches found no record of a Clarke & Shepherd (1966) Biochemical Journal 100(3), 32C-33C piece titled "The hatching factor for the potato cyst-nematode Heterodera rostochiensis," and the DOI 10.1042/bj1000032C returned no resolving record. The 32C-33C page format is consistent with a Biochemical Society meeting-abstract, which are poorly indexed online, so absence of hits is not strong enough to count as positive evidence of non-existence.

Three WebSearches for the exact title "The Supreme Court's 2018 Term: The Roberts Court's Eighth Year" combined with Chemerinsky and California Law Review returned no matching article. Chemerinsky is a real, prolific author who does write annual Supreme Court term reviews, but these appear in ABA Journal columns and other venues (e.g., Denver/Touro law reviews), not California Law Review under this exact title, and no such California Law Review piece surfaced. This is negative evidence but not definitive: it could be a real article not well-indexed by web search, or a fabricated title/venue combination. No positive evidence of existence or non-existence was found within the 3-search budget.

The book "Finite Difference Methods for Ordinary and Partial Differential Equations: Steady-State and Time-Dependent Problems" by Randall J. LeVeque, published by SIAM in 2007, is confirmed to exist with exact match on title, author, year, and venue. The cited ISBN (978-0-898716-46-8) does not match the actual ISBN (978-0-898716-29-0), but this is a minor metadata error that does not change which work is being cited, since title+author+year+venue unambiguously identify the real book.

Three WebSearch queries (full title + authors, the exact DOI, and author + journal + year) returned no trace of "The Medical Merry-Go-Round: A Sociocultural Analysis of the Medicalization of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder" by Rembis & Serlin. The DOI 10.1007/s10912-013-9270-9 does not resolve to any indexed work (search only surfaced an unrelated similarly-numbered DOI in a different journal), and no article by this title appears in Journal of Medical Humanities or elsewhere. No positive evidence of the work's existence was found in any search.
